---
title: "Scope & Definitions"
subtitle: "Applied to every variable"
date: last-modified
---

**Purpose.** Fix the boundaries and the method before characterization starts, so
results are comparable across variables and the work is repeatable. Items marked
**[CONFIRM in review]** / **[FILL]** are decisions for the science team; everything else is
drawn from the lit-review database and flagged with source IDs.

---

## 1. Datasets in scope

The two downscaling paths treat most variables **fundamentally differently**, and
the difference is the single most useful thing to know about them.

- **WRF (WUS-D03), 3 km CA convection-permitting** : the dynamical path, and the
  one that physically *simulates* the atmosphere. Native hourly output; resolves
  terrain-driven and mesoscale flow.
  *([R12](../references.qmd#R12), [R19](../references.qmd#R19); [R04](../references.qmd#R04) validation.)*
- **LOCA2 CA hybrid, 3 km** : the statistical/hybrid downscaling. Trained to reproduce
  an observational target, so it inherits that target's spatial structure rather
  than generating its own.

**[CONFIRM in review]** exact cadcat versions/paths, and whether 9 km WUS-D3 is in scope.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Not every variable is downscaled at parity.** Wind is not statistically
downscaled in LOCA2 the way temperature and precipitation are
*([R02](../references.qmd#R02))*.
:::

## 2. Extent

- **Spatial:** California 3 km domain (d03); IOU service territories as priority
  sub-regions. **[CONFIRM with review]**
- **Temporal:** 1980–2100; SSP3-7.0 primary. **[CONFIRM with review]**
- **Vertical:** surface.

## 3. What "good" means {#sec-good}

"The data is good" means different things per use case, so every variable ×
use case is scored against these dimensions explicitly rather than given a single
overall guess.

| dimension | what it captures | 
|---|---|
| **Mean bias** | absolute bias vs observations | 
| **Spatial pattern fidelity** | are the maxima in the right places? | statistical downscaling inherits a smoother field |
| **Extremes and distribution shape** | tails, and the *shape* of the distribution | 
<!-- | **Response to terrain** | does the product resolve what its grid spacing implies? | -->
<!-- | **Diurnal / seasonal structure** | timing of daily and seasonal cycles |  -->
<!-- | **Inter-variable consistency** | coherence with the other variables an index needs |  -->

---

## 4. The reference hierarchy {#sec-references}

Three tiers, ordered by what each can settle. **The order is part of the method.**

| tier | example | answers | cannot answer |
|---|---|---|---|
| **point observations** | HDP station network | Is the product right where we measured? | ocean; unobstructed high terrain; anywhere unsampled |
| **independent fine-scale model** | CONUS404 (4 km, NCAR/USGS) | Do independent models agree? | whether either is right |
| **reanalysis** | ERA5 (0.25°) | Where and when do coarse and fine diverge? | finer scale structures |

**Observations first.** A ratio against a coarse reanalysis measures a *distance*,
not an error: at 0.25° (~31 km) a reanalysis cannot represent a 3 km ridge–valley
contrast, so disagreement over terrain is expected and is not by itself evidence
against either side.

**The reanalysis earns its place through coverage.** It is the only
field that is complete and uniform, which makes it the only one that can supply a
*control region*, somewhere the mechanism under test should switch off. For wind
that is the ocean, where a resolution effect must vanish and a calibration error
must not.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**Station siting is the limiting factor, and it is not standardised.** Instrument
height usually is. Where the instrument *stands* is not, and that difference is
a large source of scatter in every station comparison. Open (exposed) sites will behave differently from sheltered ones.
:::

---

## 5. Choosing the metric {#sec-metric}

**The metric is not universal.** Decide it before any comparison is run and state
it on the characterization page. Wind speed is an unbounded variable, while
relative humidity is bounded between 0 and 100 %. 

A ratio is meaningless for a bounded variable: where observed RH is 90 %, no model
can score above 1.11 however wrong it is, so a map of RH ratio is largely a map of
where the observations are high.

Beyond a bias, two diagnostics have proved decisive and are now standard:

**Distribution analysis** examines the overall shape of the variable's distribution,
and a **quantile comparison (Q–Q against observations).** A straight line through the
origin means the departure is affine, a shift and a stretch, and a simple
correction is the right functional form. Curvature means it is not.


---

## 7. Known issues to carry in from the start

- Absolute bias and its sensitivity to model configuration.
- Complex terrain and coastal transitions, where both model error and
  observational reference are worst *([R18](../references.qmd#R18))*.
- The sparse-California-reference problem for anything trained on observations
  *([DQ9](../references.qmd#DQ9); [R16](../references.qmd#R16))*.
- Robustness of projected changes for **maxima** vs means
  *([DQ6](../references.qmd#DQ6))*; spatial consistency of trends across GWLs
  *([DQ7](../references.qmd#DQ7))*.
